messages.subject: How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
parts:
Dear all,

I have a rather simple problem for which I nevertheless do not seem to be able to find the answer (note that the following is not my actual problem, but a simpler data set illustrating the issue). 

I have a single observation from several individuals observed in several groups (the groups are actually independent experiments). My goal is to estimate the mean on the observed variable while accounting for the (random) effect of group. 

My problem is that, when entering group as random effect, the estimated mean is the weighted mean (i.e., mean of the group means), but not the unweighted mean (i.e., mean across individuals). Given that the goal is a meta-analytic assessment across groups, I want to weight each individual equally and not the groups. I figure I need to somehow weight the individual group effect by some function of the group size, but I am not able to do this properly.

My model is quite simple (data and code are given below):

data {
  int<lower=1> nsubj;
  int<lower=1> ngroup;
  int<lower=1> group[nsubj];
  real y[nsubj];
  // real esize[nsubj]; // some function of group size probably helps
}
parameters {
  real mu_mu;  
  vector[ngroup] deltahat;
  real<lower=0> sigma_i;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  real mu[nsubj];  // individual parameters
 
  for (j in 1:nsubj) {
    // add displacement to group level parameters:
    mu[j] = mu_mu + deltahat[group[j]]; // esize[j]*deltahat[group[j]] does not work...
  }
}
model {
  deltahat ~ normal(0, sigma_i);
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

Estimating this model gives the following value which is basically the weighted mean, but not the unweighted mean (which I want).

# estimated mean 
get_posterior_mean(f1, pars = "mu_mu")[,5]
# [1] 0.8839036

# weighted mean (i.e., groups weighted equally):
mean(aggregate(y~group, d, mean)$y)
# [1] 0.8834377

# unweighted mean (i.e., individuals weighted equally):
mean(d$y)
# [1] 0.8590205

Any ideas what I need to change to weight the individual data points equally and not the groups? 

Thanks,
Henrik

parts:
The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.

The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
look at calibration. Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
have the right coverage. And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
evaluation set to test real-world calibration.

Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal. Assume there
are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
g[n] in 1:K. Then the generative model is:

vector[N] y;
vector[K] mu;
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;

y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);

mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

sigma[k] ~ ...;

You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.

- Bob

Also, in my real example (which was too long to write an easily understandable mail), the data is actually not normally distributed but follows a multinomial distribution and I have multiple random effects and parameters. The random effects are each parameterized as multivariate non-centered parametrizations with mean 0 which leads to the situation that the individual predictions are something like:

mu[j]      = mu_mu[2] + deltahat[j,1] + delta2hat[group[j],3] + ...; // and then some more transformations with mu along the way...

  // real esize[nsubj]; // some function of group size probably helps
}

real<lower=0> sigma[ngroup];

The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.

The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
evaluation set to test real-world calibration.

Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:

  vector[K] mu;
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;

  y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);

  mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

  sigma[k] ~ ...;

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
parts:
Here's how to test that things are working properly.

Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
Repeat.

If that works, your model's coded properly.

When you have

y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)

you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y. Instead,
normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
in the mu[k] across groups.

The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
parts:
Hi Bob,

I understand your point and appreciate the recommendations about testing ones model. But it does not really answer my actual question, so please apologize that I come back to it.

The parameter I want to estimate is not the (unweighted) mean of the groups, but the mean of the participants (i.e., a weighted group mean). Imagine this like a meta-analysis on the individual level data. And in a meta-analysis it is common to weight the effect by the sample sizes of the individual studies. 

So if my parameterization does not allow me to estimate the value I am actually interested in (i.e., mu_mu captures the variations across groups), my question is:  How can I parameterize a model that estimates a hyper-parameter corresponding to the weighted group mean (i.e., groups weighted by their sample size) while including a random effect of group (i.e., adequately accounting for the fact that individuals within my groups might be more similar to the other group members than members of other groups) and possibly other random effects (which are not part of the simple example)?

Cheers,
Henrik

Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 23:22:26 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
Here's how to test that things are working properly.

Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
Repeat.  

If that works, your model's coded properly.

When you have

  y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)

you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y.  Instead,
normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
in the mu[k] across groups.  

The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.  

- Bob

> The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
> That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.
>
> The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
> Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
> some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
> look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
> have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
> evaluation set to test real-world calibration.
>
> Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
> are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
> g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:
>
>   vector[N] y;
>   vector[K] mu;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);
>
>   mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
>   sigma[k] ~ ...;
>
> You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
parts:
If you have a way of estimating the population distribution
of predictors, then you can do post-stratification to find
an estimate of a population quantity of interest given a model
based on the predictors. We don't really have that in the manual,
but in a simple case where you just have K groups, then you
calculate some quantity of interest per group, lets say alpha[k],
the you have some knowledge of the size of each group, say size[k].
Then you can just literally calculate the population mean for alpha
as

alpha_pop = sum(alpha .* size)

if alpha and size are both defined as K-vectors. You'd usually do
this in the generated quantities block.

A meta-analysis works the other way around, which is what I was
suggesting in early email. It works out to generate each group
as a different "experiment". But it assumes a generative model of
some population quantity of interest, which won't necessarily look
like a weighted mean.

- Bob

> On Sep 30, 2016, at 5:18 PM, Henrik Singmann <sing...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> The parameter I want to estimate is not the (unweighted) mean of the groups, but the mean of the participants (i.e., a weighted group mean). Imagine this like a meta-analysis on the individual level data. And in a meta-analysis it is common to weight the effect by the sample sizes of the individual studies.
>
> So if my parameterization does not allow me to estimate the value I am actually interested in (i.e., mu_mu captures the variations across groups), my question is: How can I parameterize a model that estimates a hyper-parameter corresponding to the weighted group mean (i.e., groups weighted by their sample size) while including a random effect of group (i.e., adequately accounting for the fact that individuals within my groups might be more similar to the other group members than members of other groups) and possibly other random effects (which are not part of the simple example)?

> Cheers,
> Henrik

> Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 23:22:26 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> Here's how to test that things are working properly.
>
> Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
> 50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
> Repeat.
>

>
> When you have
>
> y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
> mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)

>

> each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the

Except sample size isn’t always a meaningful concept
depending on your model.  If the group-level likelihoods
are not in the exponential family then there isn’t really
a formal definition of sample size so your request is
ill-posed.

That said, when you do have exponential family likelihoods
and a Gaussian hierarchical model then the hierarchical
mean already acts like a weighted mean over the groups
(modulo the regularization of the hyperprior).  Those groups
with fewer data pull the hierarchical mean less, just as
desired.

The parameter I want to estimate is not the (unweighted) mean of the groups, but the mean of the participants (i.e., a weighted group mean). So if my parameterization does not allow me to estimate the value I am actually interested in (i.e., mu_mu captures the variations across groups), my question is:  How can I parameterize a model that estimates a hyper-parameter corresponding to the weighted group mean (i.e., groups weighted by their sample size) while including a random effect of group (i.e., adequately accounting for the fact that individuals within my groups might be more similar to the other group members than members of other groups) and possibly other random effects (which are not part of the simple example)?

Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 23:22:26 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
Here's how to test that things are working properly.

Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
Repeat.  

If that works, your model's coded properly.

When you have

  y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)

you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y.  Instead,
normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
in the mu[k] across groups.  

The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.  

- Bob

> Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 15:40:38 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
> That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.
>
> The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
> Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
> some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
> look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
> have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
> evaluation set to test real-world calibration.
>
> Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
> are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
> g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:
>
>   vector[N] y;
>   vector[K] mu;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);
>
>   mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
>   sigma[k] ~ ...;
>
> You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.
>
> - Bob
